title: Saraswati in the Giant's Mouth
hookLine: the gods fear what a giant will ask for, so the goddess of speech steps into his mouth
carry: speech is sacred: saraswati lives in words
tomorrow: parvati, and a test in disguise

lines: THE GODS FEAR THE GIANT'S WISH.
cards: Three brothers have done fierce austerities for a very long time: Ravana, Vibhishana, and the giant Kumbhakarna. Brahma, the creator, is pleased, and about to grant each a boon. The gods are worried.

Ravana's request is bad enough, but Kumbhakarna is enormous and hungry, and whatever he asks for, the worlds may not survive it. So the gods bring Brahma a quiet plea: do something before the giant opens his mouth.
This path met this scene once from Kumbhakarna's side. Today, the side of the goddess who walks into it.

teach.b: In the Uttara Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana, Brahma calls Saraswati to mind, and she's there beside him.
He asks her to go and be the speech in the giant's mouth. She enters Kumbhakarna's speech, and when Brahma asks what he wants, out comes a wish to sleep, for years and years. Brahma grants it.
Then the goddess leaves him, and Kumbhakarna, himself again, realizes what he's said, and is dismayed. Look at who Saraswati is here. She doesn't fight, argue, or need a weapon.

She is speech itself, and she knows a single wish said out loud can change the shape of the world. Later tellers sharpened it into a pun: he meant to ask for Indra's throne, and the word slipped and became sleep.
That pun isn't Valmiki's, but you can see why people loved it: one sound out of place, and history turns. It's a little unsettling, too, the goddess of learning used to trip a tongue.
Under it sits an old Hindu teaching: speech, vak, is sacred and has real power.

teach.h: ONE WORD CAN CHANGE THE WORLD.
teach.b: It's why mantras are said aloud with care, and why many children learn a short prayer to say before study, beginning Saraswati namastubhyam: Saraswati, I bow to you.

teach.h: THE WEEK: DURGA, KALI, LAKSHMI, SARASWATI.
teach.b: And with that, the week closes. Durga, loved as a daughter coming home. Kali, called Ma, and Shakti dancing over still Shiva.
Lakshmi, who stays where she's honored, and chooses Vishnu. Saraswati, sacred knowledge, and sacred speech. One goddess still waits her turn: Parvati.

how: Saraswati is invoked as the goddess of speech and learning; some Hindus offer her a short prayer before study, speaking, or performance, and the story of Kumbhakarna's boon is told in Ramayana retellings and plays.

games.q: a week of goddesses: tap the pairs.

s: Kumbhakarna asked for sleep on purpose
in Valmiki's Uttara Kanda, Saraswati entered his speech; when she left, he was dismayed at what he'd said.
the Indra's-throne pun is Valmiki's own
later tellers added it; in Valmiki the goddess simply enters his speech.
Brahma calls Saraswati at the gods' request
the gods fear the giant's wish, and Brahma asks her to be the speech in his mouth.

games.q: you're Brahma. a giant is about to ask you for a boon, and the gods fear what he'll say. what do you do?
o: ask Saraswati to be the speech in his mouth
games.why: Brahma calls Saraswati; she enters Kumbhakarna's speech, and he asks to sleep.

practice: Watch your thoughts for a little while as if each were about to be said out loud, noticing the ones that would hurt and the ones that would help, without stopping any.

See the small gap between the thought and the mouth, and how much can happen in it. If you pray, say Saraswati namastubhyam, or ask her in your own words to guard your speech; if you don't, rest in the gap.

wordCard.voice: Durga. The name over a week of goddesses, met as characters: today, Saraswati, speech itself, in a giant's mouth. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vak, speech; Saraswati is linked with sacred speech, and here she becomes the speech in a giant's mouth.

carryVoice: Your line: speech is sacred, saraswati lives in words. Tomorrow, Parvati, and a test in disguise. A week, done.
